strategies.name: The 4-step client-acquisition workflow (framing)
strategies.what_it_is: The speaker's backbone for the whole video: find leads, qualify them / work out which service to offer each one, message them, then lock the deal. He says this is the exact method that got him his first client within two weeks.
steps: Step 1: find leads.
Step 2: qualify the lead, i.e. identify which service to offer them.
Step 3: message them.
Step 4: lock (close) the client.
Learn each lead source manually first, then automate it so new leads arrive daily without manual work.
strategies.claimed_result: First client within two weeks. He 'guarantees' the viewer will also get a first client within a few weeks, as long as the viewer actually puts in the effort. No followers needed and no money needed at the start; the methods are free and can be started the same day.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Needs no followers and no ad spend. He says three lead-finding methods at the start and four later, so the count is inconsistent in the transcript. The chapter list says 4 methods.

strategies.name: Checklist item 1: portfolio website with photo, story, projects, contact page, testimonials
strategies.what_it_is: A personal or portfolio site to have in place before sending a single message or email. It builds trust and lets you charge more and win more clients.
steps: Put your own photo on the site (number one item) so the client sees a real person behind it, not a bot.
Add your projects.
Write a short description: where you are from, your story, how you started. He says Western clients care about the person's story and struggle and are more likely to empathize and order.
Add an obvious contact page showing how to reach you.

Add testimonials from real customers. He also says that if you have none you could add fake ones, but make them sound realistic (this is the speaker's advice only; it is deceptive and should not be copied).
strategies.claimed_result: Higher trust, higher prices, more clients won.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Do all of this before the first message or email is sent.

strategies.name: Checklist item 2: custom domain plus business email on that domain
strategies.what_it_is: Buy your own domain and run email from it. Subdomains and Gmail make you look amateur.
steps: Buy your own domain instead of using a free subdomain like .site, .vercel or netlify subdomains. Owning a domain subconsciously signals you invested in your work and are serious.
Create an email address on that domain and send outreach from it, not from Gmail.
If you must use Gmail, at least use your real name, not a random-looking address.
He points to his own earlier video 'How to get a business email in 2026' for the process, with the link in the description.
strategies.claimed_result: Clients take you more seriously and are more likely to hire you; a subdomain lowers your perceived value.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Rule: domain, email and website must all exist together before outreach.
strategies.example_or_template: Example he shows: a cold email he received from a freelancer (named like 'Uzair bhai') claiming 4 years of experience and linking a portfolio. The work looked good, but it came from a random-looking Gmail address and a non-custom domain, so it felt less professional. He says he does not take Gmail senders seriously and most likely will not give them work, whereas he takes custom-domain senders more seriously.

strategies.name: Checklist item 3: one demo project per service, tailored to the lead's niche
strategies.what_it_is: For every service you offer, have a ready demo project or link to send, matched to the prospect's industry.
steps: Build at least one demo per service you sell.
Keep a link ready to send and say 'this is the kind of thing I will build for you'.
Pick the demo that best matches the prospect's niche when you send it.
strategies.claimed_result: The client is more likely to open the link and look at your work, and if they like it they are more likely to hire you. He says he gets cold emails offering websites with no website link at all, and anyone can claim they can build a site, so showing work is very important.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Demo must be niche-specific, not generic.
strategies.example_or_template: Bad match: pitching a clothing brand and attaching a restaurant website as the demo. That does not make sense, because it is not their industry. Send the closest-fit demo you have.

strategies.name: Checklist item 4: booking link, payment method, tracking sheet, Loom account
strategies.what_it_is: Operational basics to have ready before outreach so you can close and track.
steps: Booking link: have a link ready for a first online meeting on Zoom or Google Meet, because many clients want a call first. The scheduling tool is not named in the transcript.

Payment method: pick a way for the client to pay and have a payment link ready. Local clients can pay by bank transfer. International clients need something else. He names services that sound like Wise and Payoneer, and one that sounds like 'Remitly'. The names are garbled in the transcript, so treat them as unclear.

Tracking sheet: create a Google Sheet listing every lead and client with name, details, whether they replied and whether you followed up. Use it to compute conversion rate, for example of 100 people messaged, how many replied and how many converted. Also use it to follow up with old contacts and track total outreach.
Loom account: make an account on a video tool (sounds like Loom; garbled as 'Lo/LM'). He says he will explain how it is used for videos later in the video.
strategies.claimed_result: Conversion-rate visibility and an easy follow-up list.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Example metric: 100 messages sent, then count replies and conversions.

strategies.name: Pick the channel by target market: DMs/WhatsApp for local, email for international
strategies.what_it_is: Choose where you contact leads depending on where the lead is based.
steps: Targeting local businesses in India or Pakistan (the subcontinent): use Instagram DMs and WhatsApp. Do not use email, because he says people there do not check email and live on WhatsApp and Instagram.
Targeting international clients such as the US or the West: use email.
He says he will cover how to collect all four kinds of contact: emails, phone numbers, Instagram and WhatsApp.
strategies.claimed_result: Better response by matching the channel to the region.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Subcontinent: Instagram DM and WhatsApp. US and West: email.

strategies.name: Dynamic offers: tailor the pitch to the single need you observe in the lead
strategies.what_it_is: Do not send the same generic pitch listing all your services. Look at the prospect, identify one specific need, and offer only the service that fixes it. He says a slight difference in the pitch makes the order much more likely.
steps: Check the prospect before messaging: Google Maps listing, website, Instagram bio, posts.
Map what you observe to a specific offer (see the list under 'numbers_or_rules').
State the observation first, then the offer.
Never list everything ('I can also do websites, voice agents, chatbots...'); mention only the one service matching their need.
strategies.claimed_result: Higher chance the prospect orders because the pitch fits their actual requirement.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Observation to offer mapping given: (a) No website on Google Maps: 'I saw you on Google Maps, you have no website, I want to build you one.' (b) Has a website but it is old or badly designed: offer a new, better-designed site that improves conversion rate and SEO and brings more sales, not just 'a website'. (c) Website slow or not working on mobile: offer to make it mobile-friendly and fix SEO. (d) Instagram bio uses a Linktree: offer a real website on a custom domain that looks more professional. (e) Facebook or Instagram post with many unanswered questions or customer queries: offer a voice agent or a WhatsApp bot.
strategies.example_or_template: Restaurant with no website found on Google Maps: message says you saw them on Google Maps, they had no website, so you would like to build them one.

strategies.name: Lead-finding Method 1 (manual): Google Maps with the 'Ask Maps' AI feature
strategies.what_it_is: Use Google Maps' AI search ('Ask Maps', which he says is a new feature) to list businesses of a type in a place that lack a website but have a phone number. It is better than a plain Maps search. The speaker says Maps is the first of the lead methods; the later methods are in other parts.
steps: Decide the service and the niche, for example websites for restaurants, and a city, for example San Francisco.
Open Google Maps and use the Ask Maps feature instead of the normal search box.
Type a prompt such as: find me restaurants in San Francisco that don't have a website but have a phone number.
Review the results. The returned example shows a phone number but a missing website and no email, which makes it a good lead for a domain plus full website offer.
Ask for more with a follow-up such as 'find me 20 more'. You can ask for as many as you like, so leads are close to unlimited.
Create a Google Sheet with columns such as client or lead name, phone, and email if available. Copy each business's name and phone number into it.
Reach out manually to each one, by WhatsApp or iMessage (phone number) with the offer.
Automation of this whole flow, from finding leads to sending messages, is promised later in the video.
strategies.claimed_result: Practically unlimited leads, and the no-website restaurants with phone numbers are described as 'perfect' client prospects.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Filter to use in the prompt: no website AND has a phone number. Ask for batches such as 20 more.
strategies.example_or_template: Result shown in his demo: a diner called something like 'Ming's Diner' (name uncertain in the transcript) with a phone number, no website, no email.

strategies.name: Learn manual first, then automate
strategies.what_it_is: A principle for the lead-finding section: do each method by hand before automating it.
steps: Learn the full manual process for each method.
Then build the automation, which makes building it easier.
If the automation breaks or stops running, you will know how to debug it.
strategies.claimed_result: Easier setup and easier debugging of automations.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Order: manual first, then automation for each of the methods.

strategies.name: Google Maps manual prospecting (end of Method 1)
strategies.what_it_is: Search a local business type in a city on Google Maps, collect the results, store them, and contact each business one by one. This part of the transcript starts partway through the demo, using restaurants as the example; how the tool listed them is unclear in the transcript (he says he keeps asking it to 'find more' and it returns only 3 or 4 extra places each time).
steps: Search a business type in a city (restaurants in the demo).
Keep asking for more results; each round returns only a few places, so repeat many times (the city has plenty of restaurants).
Store every result in a list.
Reach out to each business individually, by email in his example.
Expect a low response rate and keep going anyway.
Other niches he names: barber shops, laundry services, 'different businesses'. Tip: ask Claude which kinds of businesses need websites, then search those types.
strategies.claimed_result: About 100 emails gives 5 to 10 business replies, and from those maybe 1 or 2 clients. He calls roughly 1 to 2% a good conversion rate. Clients who convert will probably pay about $1000 or more, so the effort pays back.
strategies.example_or_template: Search idea: 'restaurants', 'barber shops', 'laundry services', or any type Claude says needs a website.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: 100 emails -> 5-10 replies -> 1-2 clients; 1-2% conversion is 'good'; typical client value about $1000+. He says he will later show how to move a 2-5% figure to 5-10% (see the secret-method note). Results depend heavily on how good the message is (message content comes in a later chapter).

strategies.name: Meta Ad Library prospecting (Method 2)
strategies.what_it_is: Use Meta's public database of all active Facebook/Instagram ads to find businesses that are already paying for ads, then pick those with a visible gap (no website, a weak website, or a weak ad-to-sale funnel) and pitch the matching service. He says it is harder than the other methods but the leads are already spending money on marketing, so they are more likely to buy.
steps: Search Google for 'Meta Ad Library' and open the facebook.com ads library page.
Choose 'All ads'.

Type a keyword that hints at a business needing your service. His example: 'DM to order'. He also mentions 'contact for price' as a similar phrase. Businesses that take orders by DM probably have no website, or one that can be upgraded.
Scroll the ad results and look at the website/destination link shown under each ad.
If the ad links to Instagram.com, the advertiser has probably linked only their Instagram account. Open the link in a new tab and check whether they have a website.
Skip advertisers with a good website. Keep those with no website, or a clearly weak one, as targets.
Collect those leads and reach out individually.
Expect lots of trial and error. He did this live and unscripted.
strategies.claimed_result: No numbers claimed for this method. In the live demo, of about 5 advertisers checked, 2 or 3 looked like good prospects (one with a weak website, and one Facebook shop with only a Gmail address and social links and no website). The others already had decent sites and were skipped.
strategies.example_or_template: Search keyword 'DM to order'. Pitch for advertisers with no site: 'we will build you a website'. Pitch for advertisers who already have a site and ads: improve conversion on the ads they already pay for, for example a voice-agent follow-up, or an automation that sends an email or message the moment someone clicks through from the ad to the website.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Rule: identify one signal that suggests the lead needs your specific service, such as no website for a web-design offer. For a voice-agent or AI-consulting offer, look for the thing that would make them need it. The transcript gives no volume or conversion numbers.

strategies.name: Instagram bio search (Method 3)
strategies.what_it_is: Search Instagram bios for signals that someone could use your service. He says this cannot be done by hand and will be covered in the automation section with Apify and Zapier. Here he only explains the idea.
steps: Use automation (Apify to scrape, Zapier to process; both covered later in the video) to search Instagram bios.
Look at what the bio reveals. His example is a bio that links to a Linktree instead of a real website, which suggests the person might want a website.
Offer the matching service, for example 'I will build you a website'.
strategies.claimed_result: No numbers. He says people with such bios could be interested, though he personally is not because his work is different. He says to definitely try it.
strategies.example_or_template: Signal example: bio link is a Linktree page rather than a website.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Needs the later automation steps (Apify and Zapier). The exact search or filter settings are not given in this part.

strategies.name: LinkedIn Sales Navigator Core with filters (Method 4)
strategies.what_it_is: Use LinkedIn Sales Navigator to build a filtered list of decision-makers at small companies, mainly for B2B and international clients. He says these clients are harder to win but pay well; the figure he gives is garbled in the transcript (it reads like '$1000 or $2000' per client, unclear).
steps: Sign up for the LinkedIn Premium free trial of Sales Navigator Core (the button reads 'Try for $0'; choose a goal such as finding and reaching prospective clients; the option you pick does not matter).

Enter payment details. He says you are not charged during the trial, but you must cancel before it ends (he mentions cancelling around day 25) or you will be billed. After the trial the price is about $90 a month, which he calls quite expensive.
Open Sales Navigator, go to Search, then Lead filters and Account filters.

Set the filters for your offer. His example offer is a voice agent for small companies: Company headquarters = United States (optional; any country works); Current job title = Founder and Co-founder (small companies, where the owner decides); Industry = e.g. dentists, or the broader Healthcare; Company headcount = 1-10 and 11-50.
Review the leads shown.
Contact them either directly inside LinkedIn, or export to Apollo (see the next strategy).
strategies.claimed_result: He says the filters returned a good list of leads. If you do land these clients, he says the trial cost is easily offset by what they pay.
strategies.example_or_template: Voice-agent example: HQ United States; titles Founder and Co-founder; industry dentists or healthcare; headcount 1-10 and 11-50.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Headcount sweet spot is 1-10 and 11-50: small enough to outsource to freelancers and big enough to have a budget. A company with no employees likely has no budget, and big companies are less likely to buy. Sales Navigator Core says 'over 50 search filters'. Cost is about $90 a month after a 1-month free trial. Direct LinkedIn messages are capped at 50 a month.

strategies.name: Apollo.io for unlimited outreach to LinkedIn leads
strategies.what_it_is: Because LinkedIn caps direct messages at about 50 a month, take the people found in Sales Navigator and look up their email addresses and phone numbers with Apollo.io, then contact them outside LinkedIn without that cap.
steps: Build the lead list in LinkedIn Sales Navigator.
Use Apollo.io to find each lead's email address and phone number.
Message them individually by email or phone, with no message cap.
For a full Apollo and Sales Navigator tutorial he points to a video called 'How to Start an AI Automation Agency' by someone he calls Ali (link to be in the description). He will not re-cover it.
strategies.claimed_result: He calls this a very good option. No numbers given.
strategies.example_or_template: Not given in this part.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: LinkedIn limit is 50 messages a month; Apollo removes that limit. Apollo pricing is not given.

strategies.name: Credibility checklist before any outreach
strategies.what_it_is: Repeated rule that every channel you reach out from must look professional before you send a single message, or prospects will not reply.
steps: Make your LinkedIn profile professional.
Put your portfolio and every project on it, so you have proof of work.
Make sure the email and any other outreach channel are fully set up and look right.
Only then start messaging.
strategies.claimed_result: He says without credibility and proof of work people will not take you seriously or hire you, and outreach is wasted because they will not reply.
strategies.example_or_template: Not given.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Applies to every channel you use, not just LinkedIn.

steps: Open Claude or ChatGPT.
Describe your offer and ask which Sales Navigator filters you should use.
Apply the suggested filters in Sales Navigator.

strategies.name: Let Claude choose the Sales Navigator filters (LinkedIn Sales Navigator, end of the method)

steps: Tell Claude your situation, the service you offer and who your audience is. His example target: healthcare companies, individual clinics and individual doctor offices.

Claude replies with specific filter options. He names job titles such as practice manager and office manager to enter in the job-title field. It also gives separate 'lead filters' and 'account filters'.
Enter those filters directly into Sales Navigator and pull the leads.
The speaker's point about quality: LinkedIn gives more professional, more useful people than other sources.
strategies.claimed_result: No numeric result. He says Claude gave 'very specific options' and that this should be good enough to start from.
strategies.example_or_template: Prompt content, paraphrased: here is my situation, here is the service I offer, here is my audience (healthcare companies, individual clinics, doctor offices); tell me which filters to apply. Example titles in the output: practice manager, office manager.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Job titles go in the job-title filter, and the lead and account filters are applied together. Claude's full list is not read out in this part.

strategies.what_it_is: A cost note and a tactic about LinkedIn Sales Navigator. Leads there are not free, and he recommends extracting as many as you can in the first (trial) month.
steps: Budget about $100 a month for Sales Navigator.
In the first month, pull as many leads as you can.
He says a new account could be used to get another trial, but he personally does not recommend it because of legal problems. Only mentioned as something others could do.

strategies.name: Automated lead-finding stack: Apify plus Zapier
strategies.what_it_is: A two-tool setup that finds leads automatically and files them in a Google Sheet. Apify does the scraping and Zapier connects it to Google Sheets. He also says it can later connect to email or WhatsApp outreach.
steps: Create an Apify account (link in the video description).
Create a Zapier account (link in the description).
Build the scrape first in Apify, then the automation in Zapier, then a Google Sheet to hold the leads.
If you don't want to pay anything, do the same work by hand (slower). If you want to save time, you pay.
strategies.claimed_result: The finished demo sheet holds restaurant names and phone numbers. He says Apify can also return emails and other details.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Zapier: roughly a one-month free trial, then about $20 a month. He advises cancelling before billing if it isn't useful. Apify: $5 free credit at the start, then pay as you go. He says the $5 gives you 'a good amount' of leads. These costs are his estimates, spoken loosely ('I believe').

strategies.name: Scrape Google Maps for businesses with no website (Apify)
strategies.what_it_is: Use an Apify Google Maps scraper to pull local businesses in a chosen city, filtered to those with no website. The idea is that they are the potential clients for web or digital services. His demo target was restaurants in New York.
steps: Open the Apify console and go to the Apify Store.
Search 'maps'. Several Google Maps scrapers appear. He picks the one with the most reviews (about 1,800 reviews, 4.7 rating, versus another with about 200), reasoning that more reviews means better.
Open the actor page. It shows price and output fields.
Click 'Use Actor'. Fill the input: search term 'restaurant', location 'New York', number of places 10 for the test (more places cost more).
Open 'Add on search filters and categories' and set the website filter to 'scrape places without a website'.
Click Save and Start. The run returns the restaurants.
He only needs two fields, name and phone. The actor also gives address and, optionally, menu and opening hours.
Run it once so that Zapier can import that run in the next step.
strategies.claimed_result: The 10-place test run returned a good list of restaurants with names and phone numbers.
strategies.example_or_template: Input used: search = restaurant, location = New York, count = 10, filter = no website.

Click the 'Booking pages' option.

Set your availability.

Set the appointment duration, for example 30 minutes.
Finish the settings, press Next and save.
Copy the link it gives you and attach it to your offer message.

strategies.name: Free-first offer: the client pays only after seeing the result
strategies.what_it_is: Offer to do the work (or a demo) for free first, and the client pays only if they like the result. He calls it a very good tactic for beginners with few portfolio projects and little social proof, but only for Western clients.
steps: Say in the pitch that they only pay after they see the result.
Build the demo or work for them first.
Show them the result.
If they like it, they pay; only then hand over the real website (see the payment terms strategy).
strategies.claimed_result: He says Western clients are generally honest. Even if they don't love the result, many will still pay because they see you put in effort, and if they like it they pay willingly. No numbers.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: Use it for Western clients (US and similar). Do NOT do this with clients in India or Pakistan: he says people will take the website and run, and you will lose your work for free.

strategies.name: The 'secret sauce': a personalized 1-2 minute video for every lead
strategies.what_it_is: He calls this a game changer for conversion. Record a short screen-share video made for that one lead and send it with the message.
steps: Record a 1 to 2 minute video for each lead.
Show the lead's website on screen. If they have no website, show their Google Maps listing instead.
Explain which points you would highlight and how you would build their website.
Keep your face camera on at the bottom of the screen to build trust.
Record with Loom (mentioned earlier in the video) or OBS (he is using OBS to record this video).
Attach or link the video in your email or message.
strategies.claimed_result: Shows effort and proves a real person is behind the service, not a bot or automated message, so he says conversion rates go up a lot ('trust me'). He says he has personally received 2 to 3 such videos and replied to every one and discussed the service.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: 1 to 2 minutes long. It does not scale: realistic volume is about 10, 15 or 20 leads a day, because each video is made one by one. He recommends it especially for beginners with a weak portfolio or little social proof. No conversion percentages given.

Say you can make tweaks for them.
Discuss the specific cost and pricing with them.

strategies.name: Follow-up cadence: two follow-ups at day 3 and day 7, then stop
strategies.what_it_is: Never send just one email. Follow up exactly twice, then leave the lead alone.

Follow up a first time 3 days later.
Follow up a second time 7 days later.
Stop after that.
Use Claude to write the follow-up: ask it for a follow-up email after three days that slightly modifies the pitch and makes it more attractive. He says it gave three options to choose from.
Accept rejection and non-replies as normal and do not take stress over it.
strategies.claimed_result: Reasons he gives: the first email may have been missed, or the pitch may not have been understood, so a tweaked pitch gives a second chance. He says you will get a lot of rejection and have to accept it.

strategies.name: Payment terms: 50% deposit, with a beginner exception
strategies.what_it_is: His final pricing rule on when to get paid, and how to protect trust when you are new.
steps: As a rule, take a 50% deposit up front, before delivering the website.
Beginner exception: if you are new, especially with international clients, show the finished result first and then expect payment. He says this lets the client trust you and not suspect you.
After the client has seen the result and agrees, take the payment, and only then deliver the real thing: host the website on the domain and hand over everything.
As you collect multiple clients, gradually start asking for the 50% deposit up front.
strategies.claimed_result: He says you might get burned once or twice, which is not a big problem, and that doing the work first gives the client full trust in you.
strategies.numbers_or_rules: 50% deposit up front. He clarifies that 'deliver' means showing the result, not handing over the full website, domain and hosting before payment.

strategies.name: Daily action task: list 20 businesses on Google Maps

Do 20 on the first day; he says not to do more than 20.
Keep doing it consistently so the results add up; replies and then clients will come eventually.
Work manually at first to learn, then add automations step by step and eventually automate the whole lead-mining process.
strategies.claimed_result: Eventually you will start getting responses and then clients. No timeline or numbers given.
